C18 The Canon · Reading Layer

Information & Communication

Lesson Lectures · learn

Communication looks like one skill, but it's really a pipe with three places it can fail. A message can be distorted in transit (the channel is noisy), distorted in display (the chart lies or buries its point), or distorted by emotion (the human on the other end stops listening). This cluster gives you a precise instrument for each failure mode — a 1948 engineering theorem that defines information itself, a 1983 grammar for showing data honestly, and two field-tested playbooks for the conversations where stakes are high and tempers are higher. The throughline: getting a message to land is a discipline, not a knack. Tap the cards, the diagrams, and the quizzes as you go.

1 · What information actually is: the reduction of uncertainty

Before you can transmit a message well, you have to know what a message even is. Claude Shannon answered that in A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948) — and his answer was radical: information has nothing to do with meaning. In his own recorded words:

"To measure information you have to look at it without regard to meaning — that upset a lot of people, that content is irrelevant. The point of sending a message is to remove uncertainty: something you didn't know, now you know."

— Discern, "Claude Shannon Explains Information Theory" · in your corpus

So information = surprise. A message you could have predicted carries zero information; the more surprising it is, the more it tells you. Shannon's unit is the bit — the uncertainty of one fair coin toss — and the rule is brutally simple: "if something's completely predictable there's zero information; if something's completely random you need information about everything."

Information = how much uncertainty a message removes  ·  predictable → 0 bits

The Computerphile explainer shows why surprise is measured with a logarithm — so that rare events score high without "going off the scale": "every time you halve the probability you only increase the amount you're surprised by by literally a bit." The average surprise of a source is its entropy — which Art of the Problem reframes beautifully as the expected number of yes/no questions you'd have to ask to pin the message down.

2 · Noise, redundancy, and "if you said it once, you haven't said it"

Real channels are noisy — distraction, competing messages, garbled wires. Shannon's second gift is the cure: redundancy is not waste, it's error-correction. Re-encoding the signal is how it survives the channel. This is the entire mathematics behind why an important message must be sent more than once, in more than one form. The corpus grounds it in working engineering, not metaphor:

"A lot of concepts in computer science are directly derived from this — things like compression, zip files, network error-correction codes or error-detection… are all directly related to information theory."

— Computerphile, "Why Information Theory is Important" · in your corpus

There's also a hard ceiling. Every channel has a capacity — a maximum bits-per-second it can reliably carry — and you cannot beat it: "if you know the throughput in bits of a channel… there's no smart way of putting more information through it than whatever that number is." Below that ceiling lives entropy, the floor: you "can never do better than this on average" when compressing.

The leadership translation (and the trap): most communication fails because the channel is noisy, so the fix is intentional redundancy — say the important thing several ways, through several channels. If you said it once, you haven't said it. But redundancy has a ceiling too: past a point, repetition becomes noise (when everything is "urgent," nothing is). And remember Shannon's own warning — the math guarantees the bits arrive, never that the idea was any good.

Because it isolates a failure mode you'd otherwise blame on people. When a strategy doesn't stick, the instinct is "my team didn't get it." Shannon reframes it: the channel was noisy and you sent the message once. That's a fixable transmission problem, not a competence problem. The discipline is to separate two questions you usually blur together — did the bits arrive? (Shannon's domain: redundancy, channels) and was the idea good and persuasive? (a different domain entirely — structure, narrative, the next books on the shelf). Solve transmission first; you can't persuade with a message that never landed.

3 · Showing it: Tufte and the discipline of honest data

Words are one channel; charts are another — and they have their own grammar. Edward Tufte's The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983) treats data visualization as a cognitive discipline whose entire job is to respect the reader's eye. His frame for the whole field:

"The goal of analytical design is to make people smarter. A good start is to make our information displays worthy of the routine capabilities of the human eye-brain system."

— Tech@State, keynote by Dr. Edward Tufte · in your corpus

The eye is astonishingly high-bandwidth — Tufte notes the optic nerve carries roughly 10 megabits per second — so under-loaded displays waste the reader. His evidence is pointed: an ESPN sports table averages "150 to 200 numbers… per table," while "the average number of numbers on the government slide is 12." Push data density up; strip chartjunk out. The mechanism is the data-ink ratio:

"A large share of ink on a graphic should present data… data-ink is the non-erasable core of a graphic — the non-redundant ink arranged in response to variation in the numbers."

— Erik B, "Edward Tufte Principles" lecture · in your corpus

But the rule the corpus rates above erasing junk is honesty. Graphical excellence starts with not lying — no truncated axes, no area-for-length tricks (Tufte's "lie factor"), no cherry-picking:

"Number one is that our graphs should display our data honestly… we don't predetermine the outcome we want and then cherry-pick the data… we let the data speak for themselves."

— Research By Design, "Graphical EXCELLENCE: Presenting Data Clearly by Tufte" · in your corpus

And the practitioner's caution against minimalism-as-vanity: "no one is that impressed by how pretty you make your chart." Erase junk in service of the message — substance over design — not as an aesthetic end. A light reference line, a label, a touch of color that aids a non-expert reader is not chartjunk; it's redundancy doing Shannon's job on the visual channel.

4 · The human channel goes crucial

The noisiest channel of all is a person whose emotions are running. Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler's Crucial Conversations (2002) names the exact moment a conversation turns crucial: when stakes are high, opinions differ, and emotions run strong. Under those conditions people stop transmitting meaning and default to silence (withdraw, avoid, sugarcoat) or violence (control, label, attack). The book's central reframe is that those reactions are not the problem to argue with — they're a signal:

"This book challenges us to see silence or violence as a sign that the other person isn't feeling safe to talk… When we see this we have to stop ourselves and ask, what can I do to restore safety?"

— Therapy in a Nutshell, "Crucial Conversations Book Summary" · in your corpus

The key move is counterintuitive: when the conversation gets heated, you don't push harder on content — you stop and repair safety, via mutual purpose ("we're on the same side") and mutual respect. The corpus dramatizes it. A manager, Esther, must confront a designer, Leia, about a client problem; Leia bristles — "Are you questioning my design skills?" — and Esther defuses it with a contrasting statement (clarify what you don't mean, then what you do):

"Oh, no, no — that's not it at all. I have no concerns with the quality of your work. Your past work speaks for itself. I'm just trying to figure out if there's a disconnect…"

— Crucial Learning, "Crucial Conversations for Mastering Dialogue: What to Expect" · in your corpus

Safety restored, the real cause surfaces — the specs were wrong — instead of a blame spiral. And the cost of not doing this is measurable: co-author Joseph Grenny's study of 1,100 employees found "43% estimated they waste 2 weeks or more ruminating about an unresolved problem at work," and "one in three estimate their inability to speak up… has cost their organization at least $25,000."

5 · The three conversations hiding in every hard one

Its sister book — Stone, Patton & Heen's Difficult Conversations (1999, from the Harvard Negotiation Project) — adds the diagnostic layer. Every difficult conversation is really three conversations at once, and most people try to have only the first, then are baffled when it fails:

  • The "What Happened" conversation — facts, interpretations, blame. The move: from who's right to each person's story; from blame to contribution.
  • The Feelings conversation — the emotions driving behavior that go unspoken. Name them, or they "run the conversation from underneath."
  • The Identity conversation — what this says about me: am I competent, am I a good person? This is why hard talks feel threatening. (Leia's "Are you questioning my design skills?" is a pure identity reaction.)

The skill is to spot which layer is actually live and shift from certainty to curiosity — replace "you did X" with "I experienced X; help me understand your perspective." Notice this is the same unlock as Crucial Conversations under a different name: surface the feeling/identity threat, or it silently steers everything. And both books carry the same warning — these are skills you must run live, under stress, which is precisely when it's hardest:

"Human beings tend to behave their worst in the most critical moment… when you're under stress, blood is directed away from your brain into your muscles, so your thinking naturally suffers."

— Successful By Design, "Crucial Conversations Summary & Review (ANIMATED)" · in your corpus

6 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

The exact terms the canon uses. Tap a card to flip it.

7 · One mental model, four failure modes

Stack the four books and a single picture appears: a message must survive transmission, display, and emotion to land. Each book guards one gate. Tap each layer.

Worked example — announcing a reorg. You have to tell your team their reporting lines are changing. Transmission (Shannon): don't fire one all-staff email and assume it landed — the channel is noisy. Send the core message three ways: a live all-hands, a written FAQ, and a 1:1 from each manager. Redundancy is the error-correction. Display (Tufte): if you show the new org chart, make it honest and dense — no 3-D boxes, no decorative gradients; one clean diagram beats six busy slides. Safety (Crucial Conversations): in the room, people will go silent (shut down) or violent (attack the plan). Read that as a safety signal, not insubordination; open with contrasting — "This is not about anyone's performance; it is about getting closer to customers." Diagnosis (Difficult Conversations): the loud objection about "logistics" (What-Happened) is usually masking an Identity fear — "does this mean I'm being demoted?" Name that layer with curiosity and the real conversation can finally happen.

8 · Check yourself

In Shannon's theory, which message carries the most information?

Information = uncertainty removed = surprise. A perfectly predictable message carries zero bits; the lower the probability of what you learn, the more information it conveys. Length and beauty are irrelevant to the math — "content is irrelevant."

For Tufte, the very first quality of graphical excellence is:

Honesty ranks above even erasing chartjunk. "We don't predetermine the outcome we want and then cherry-pick the data." A pretty chart that distorts (a high lie factor) fails the first test; "no one is that impressed by how pretty you make your chart."

A teammate goes quiet and defensive mid-conversation. The Crucial Conversations move is to:

Silence or violence is a safety signal, not data to argue with. Stop pushing content and restore safety — mutual purpose, mutual respect, a contrasting statement ("I have no concerns with your work… I'm trying to…"). Then the real issue surfaces.

⚠️ Fidelity is not persuasion — don't over-literalize the math

The seductive error is treating Shannon as a theory of communication in the everyday sense. It isn't. The 1948 math is deliberately about transmission, not meaning — Shannon said so himself: "content is irrelevant." It certifies that the bits survive a noisy channel; it says nothing about whether the message persuades, whether the chart's story is the right one, or whether the idea deserved transmitting. A perfectly transmitted bad message is still bad. The same purity trap snares Tufte: maximal data-ink is not always maximal comprehension — a non-expert sometimes needs the reference line, the label, the splash of color you were told to erase. Use these tools to get the message through cleanly; use judgment, narrative, and structure to make it worth getting through.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the rest of the shelf

Notice the same word kept reappearing across four very different books: redundancy. Shannon calls repetition error-correction; Tufte allows redundant ink when it aids the reader; Crucial Conversations has you re-state mutual purpose; Difficult Conversations has you name a layer out loud that everyone already half-feels. Saying the thing again, in another form, is not a failure of economy — it is how meaning beats noise, whether the noise is electrical, visual, or emotional. The deepest communication skill isn't eloquence; it's recognizing which channel is corrupting your message — the wire, the page, or the person — and applying the right redundancy. That recognition is the throughline into structure and narrative (Minto, Duarte), into command intent (Bungay's alignment gap), and into the negotiation and leadership shelves, where the same skill decides whether anyone follows you.

🎯 Your move

Take your single most important current message — a strategy, a change, a piece of feedback. On paper, run it through all four gates: (1) Transmission — are you relying on one channel? Re-send the same core idea two more ways, worded differently, and assume it hasn't landed yet. (2) Display — if there's a chart, delete every non-data mark (gridlines, 3-D, gradients) and check the axis for a lie factor. (3) Safety — if it's a live conversation, write one contrasting statement that defuses the biggest fear ("This is not X; it is Y"). (4) Diagnosis — name which of the three conversations (What-Happened, Feelings, Identity) is really driving the other person, and open with curiosity about their story, not your verdict.

Crucial Conversations Book Summary: How to Make It Safe to Talk About Anything signal 4
Therapy in a Nutshell · 9:34 · 85,300 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,775 words

I recently listened to Crucial Conversations on audio and honestly I did not expect that much out of it I thought it would be this short behavior based communication skill book and instead I found it full of depth on how to improve difficult conversations. In this summary I'm going to share the essence of how Crucial Conversations teaches you to have good dialogue by making it safe to talk about anything, and I'm gonna share the five most important things I learned from Crucial Conversations. Now like I said I didn't&nbsp; expect much out of this book I&nbsp; thought it would be another skills based approach that teaches the right words to say to basically manipulate others into doing what you want.

But in the long run that approach I don't believe is very effective. So I went into this book not really expecting much of it and instead I found a depth of theory that from my therapy perspective was half way between Sue Johnson's emotion focused therapy and John Gottman's approach which include things like seven principles for making marriage work and the four horsemen and etc. So from my totally therapy centered approach I saw this book is all about creating safety so that problems could be solved. Because this book goes deeper than behavior I think it offers real solutions to improving relationships and managing intensely emotional conversations.

So let's jump in to some of the essential skills. So the first one is remember your goal. So this first skill is to continually remind yourself of your goal which is to share a conversation and to solve a problem and not allow yourself to get sidetracked by switching goals. So a lot of times we get caught up in contention like needing to be right needing to win needing to punish others needing to be justified. So instead this book encourages you to keep in mind the question what do I want for myself and for others and for the relationship. So for example when having a discussion with a teenager about curfew instead of getting locked up in what time they have to be home continually remind yourself and them that what you really want is for them to be safe and for you to be able to trust them to be responsible.

They also want to be trusted and seen as responsible because that comes with freedoms. So that shared goal of mutual trust can get you on the same team as you work to figure out what time they should be home. Number two, watch for signs of stress. So learn to look for signs of crucial conversations and signs of stress within yourself. When you notice yourself getting heated take a deep breath actively calm yourself and remind yourself to stick to the goal which is shared dialogue and shared meaning. This step is basically learning to be responsive instead of reactive to the situation. Number three, give yourself more options.

So let go of false dichotomies. In therapy we call this black-and-white thinking. So for example I either had to let the boss walk all over me or I had to rudely embarrass him. I had to say nothing or I would lose my job. So instead of these dichotomies instead of you know this black-and-white thinking, you ask yourself to step back and really consider, are there truly no other options is there anyone in the company who uses a different strategy or approach for dealing with that situation? And your goal is to relax a little bit and invite creativity and flexibility. My dad once told me the story of a college president who during the Vietnam War he was struggling to know how to deal with the protesters on his campus.

He had one group who wanted to burn the American flag to show their anger about the draft and the war and he had the football team who was surrounding the flag to protect it. As tensions were rising violence seemed imminent and in similar situations other universities sent in riot police or the National Guard and this led to escalating tension and injuries and deaths. But this university president stepped back took a look at the situation and made an offer. What if we wash the flag. A symbolic move that both shows respect and the need for improvement and because of his willingness to look for that third option the situation was resolved peacefully.

Number four, check how you see others. This was my number one take away. Whenever someone reverts to silence like shutting down withdrawing going quiet or violence like aggression raising their voice or arguing. Our natural reaction is to respond more forcefully arguing our point or getting frustrated that they won't participate and instead this book challenges us to see silence or violence as a sign that the other person isn't feeling safe to talk. They feel like their point isn't being considered and they get into a fight or flight mode. When we see this we have to stop ourselves and ask what can I do to restore safety?

Crucial Conversations suggest some practical steps to restoring safety. So they need to know that you care about them and their interests so show them respect check yourself am I listening am I validating am I acting defensive or being condescending or sarcastic? Am I showing them that I value hearing what they are saying even if I don't agree? Now I think this step is really powerful because we can actively create a safe environment by how we treat the other person. When people feel that you care about them and value them it invites them to relax and be able to absorb what you're saying and share what they need to.

So it makes it more likely that you'll have a successful conversation that actually solves problems. Number five, creating safety a big part to restoring safety is working on yourself. But there are some other skills that are pretty straightforward to help others feel safe understood and valued. So one of these is front-loading. This is starting off conversations gently when a topic is crucial we tend to get nervous and go into it like tightly after avoiding it for a while so instead lead in gently. For example, there's something I'd like to get your opinion on but I'm worried that you'll be upset if I bring it up.

Front loading can help a conversation go better right from the start. Here's another one, point out you agree on highlight the areas you share instead of only focusing on the parts you disagree with. Keep pointing out your common goal for example, I really want to be able to work well with you this relationship is more important or let's see how we can solve this in a way that everyone can accept. If you need to make a tentative guess about what they're feeling upset about but not in a judgmental way. So for example you could say, it sounds like you're feeling like your opinion isn't being heard.

Number six, master your stories. So this sixth chapter on mastering your stories it's like this combination of the book leadership and self-deception and narrative therapy and a little bit of CBT thrown in for good measure. But basically it tries to help you see when you're interpreting situations in a way that harms the process. Stories are our assumptions of why people are doing what they're doing. For example, seeing yourself as the victim or blaming others as being lazy or selfish are types of stories that we tell ourselves. Distorting the facts by exaggerating their wrongs or highlighting their strengths is why these stories become problematic.

Now I thought this chapter was on point but to me it feels like a couple of books worth of information in one short chapter. So I wonder if people are actually able to absorb it in small doses or if it is better addressed in more depth. Regardless you should check yourself for signs of this. Do you have repeating patterns at work like why is everyone out to get me or all bosses are authoritarian a-holes or I'm the only hard worker around here. When you see your underlying stories for what they are, stories, then you can see past them and solve real problems. Try to replace defensiveness with curiosity.

This is something that I struggle with and this book frames this in an interesting way, when faced with someone who seems to be getting angry shutting down or being irrational rather than ask what's the worst most personal way I can take this which leads to defensiveness we should ask why would a reasonable rational and decent person think or feel this way? Leading to curiosity it's hard to feel defensive and curious at the same time. Assuming that they're doing the best they can can help us understand their obstacles to having a dialogue around crucial issues. When it comes down to it what I appreciated most about this book was its emphasis on creating real safety by giving me the responsibility to create that safe environment and it teaches the tools to make that happen.

Thanks for watching and if you found this content helpful please consider sharing it with someone who also might find it helpful. Take care.

Stakes are high, opinions&nbsp; vary, and the parties involved have strong&nbsp;&nbsp; emotions. And we've all had at least a few of&nbsp; those in our lives, even if we didn't realize&nbsp;&nbsp; it at the time. And make no mistake, crucial&nbsp; conversation is not a planned high-level&nbsp;&nbsp; meeting like the one you might have at work during&nbsp; let's say your scheduled yearly manager meeting.&nbsp;&nbsp; Crucial conversations are things like ending a&nbsp; relationship, giving your boss critical but needed&nbsp;&nbsp; feedback, or something like confronting a coworker&nbsp; or a neighbor about something that they did. &nbsp; The problem with such high stake&nbsp; conversations is that we often plain suck at&nbsp;&nbsp; having them.

We tend to avoid these conversations&nbsp; because we're afraid we're going to make matters&nbsp;&nbsp; worse. We tend to react negatively when put into&nbsp; a crucial conversation, for the simple reason that&nbsp;&nbsp; we're human, and human beings tend to behave their&nbsp; worst in the most critical moment, as the author&nbsp;&nbsp; puts it herself. After all, when you're under&nbsp; stress, blood is directed away from your brain&nbsp;&nbsp; into your muscles, so your thinking naturally&nbsp; suffers. You're also most likely caught off guard,&nbsp;&nbsp; so your first reaction might even surprise you&nbsp; when you analyze it later on.

Plus, you're lacking&nbsp;&nbsp; the right tools to handle such conversation. After&nbsp; all, crucial conversations 101 is not something&nbsp;&nbsp; that is taught in schools or university. You've&nbsp; got to figure out stuff by yourself. So let's&nbsp;&nbsp; fix all this and arm you with the right skills&nbsp; needed to handle any crucial conversation, because&nbsp;&nbsp; eventually you're going to find yourself in one,&nbsp; or you have to deliver one, no doubt about it. &nbsp; It all starts with knowing your heart. First and&nbsp; foremost, you absolutely need to stay focused on&nbsp;&nbsp; what you really want in a conversation, and none&nbsp; of the petty BS stuff like winning the argument,&nbsp;&nbsp; but the big picture item, like having a&nbsp; stronger relationship or a better job.&nbsp;&nbsp; Of course, this is not easy, and you might&nbsp; need to reverse some of the tactics that&nbsp;&nbsp; you grew up with, such as silent treatment or&nbsp; manipulation, or having to quote unquote win.&nbsp;&nbsp; You're not in a competitive sport, so&nbsp; winning the conversation might mean losing&nbsp;&nbsp; the relationship.

So always keep that in mind.&nbsp; Avoid trying to discredit the other person or&nbsp;&nbsp; put them in their place, as they say, as those,&nbsp; again, put you away from the original purpose.&nbsp;&nbsp; Remember what you really want. If the other party&nbsp; says something you disagree with, take a pause,&nbsp;&nbsp; remind yourself of what you really want, reboot,&nbsp; and get back into conversation. Uncomfortable?&nbsp;&nbsp; For sure, but exponentially better than going&nbsp; on the offense with a knee jerk reaction. &nbsp; Next, you absolutely need to ensure safety. One&nbsp; of the main prerequisites of a healthy dialogue&nbsp;&nbsp; is safety.

You cannot have a really constructive&nbsp; conversation if not all parties feel it's a safe&nbsp;&nbsp; environment. To maintain that crucial safety, you&nbsp; need to consider two core elements, what is being&nbsp;&nbsp; discussed and what is happening in response?&nbsp; Both content and conditions are important,&nbsp;&nbsp; and it makes sense when you put yourself in&nbsp; that situation. If the conditions are safe,&nbsp;&nbsp; you can say almost anything and it's going to&nbsp; be perceived semi-okay, even if it's something&nbsp;&nbsp; really bad. People typically become defensive not&nbsp; because of what is being said, AKA the content,&nbsp;&nbsp; but how they feel, or if they feel it's a safe&nbsp; place.

If you know the other person has your&nbsp;&nbsp; best interest in mind, you have no doubt about&nbsp; it, you're going to be that much more open to&nbsp;&nbsp; receiving even truly negative feedback. So how do you make the conditions safe?&nbsp;&nbsp; Well, there's four parts to it. First is&nbsp; spot the turning point. That is, notice&nbsp;&nbsp; when the conversation becomes crucial. That can&nbsp; be something physical. For instance, a person's&nbsp;&nbsp; shoulders may tense up. It could be emotional,&nbsp; when someone becomes angry or afraid or hurt, or&nbsp;&nbsp; behavioral, if someone raises a voice or becomes&nbsp; quiet.

Two is watch for signs of safety problems.&nbsp;&nbsp; When people begin to feel unsafe, they may push,&nbsp; insult, become sarcastic, or make fun of you.&nbsp;&nbsp; Instead of fighting back, try to see the other&nbsp; person's aggression as a sign that they don't feel&nbsp;&nbsp; safe. Be curious, rather than angry or fearful.&nbsp; Three, see if others are moving towards silence or&nbsp;&nbsp; verbal violence, and four, beware of&nbsp; reverting to your own style under stress,&nbsp;&nbsp; by paying close attention to what you're doing&nbsp; and the impact it is having. Are you withdrawing&nbsp;&nbsp; yourself?

Are you masking things up with jokes&nbsp; or sarcasm? Knowing yourself and how you tend to&nbsp;&nbsp; react under pressure, and trying to improve&nbsp; on that, is crucial to any conversation. &nbsp; Next is step number three. You need to make the&nbsp; content safe. For people to feel safe in speaking&nbsp;&nbsp; what is really on their minds, two things need&nbsp; to exist, a common purpose and mutual respect.&nbsp;&nbsp; Typically, when someone doesn't feel safe saying&nbsp; something which is potentially negative, but&nbsp;&nbsp; nevertheless true, it is because of two things.&nbsp; Either they don't trust the mutual purpose,&nbsp;&nbsp; and think of the last time you talked to someone&nbsp; and had a vibe that there's an ulterior motive,&nbsp;&nbsp; or the mutual respect has been undermined.&nbsp; And think of the last eye roll that you&nbsp;&nbsp; received or did, and the dialogue cannot really&nbsp; resume until that respect has been restored.&nbsp;&nbsp; Common purpose, mutual respect,&nbsp; absolutely crucial to any conversation. &nbsp; So start by asking yourself what do&nbsp; others believe you care about their goals,&nbsp;&nbsp; and if they can trust your motives.

If you don't&nbsp; genuinely care, but you're trying to get your way,&nbsp;&nbsp; quote, unquote, others will quickly see that,&nbsp; and that destroys the entire conversation.&nbsp;&nbsp; After that, having respect for the other person&nbsp; as a human being, and focus on things that make&nbsp;&nbsp; you similar, rather than different, and&nbsp; you should be in a much better spot. &nbsp; Once safety in conditions and content has&nbsp; been ensured, let's move on to the next part,&nbsp;&nbsp; and that is controlling your emotions. By learning&nbsp; to better control your emotions, you'll be in a&nbsp;&nbsp; much better position to use all the tools we've&nbsp; covered so far.

But what really are emotions?&nbsp;&nbsp; These are generally the stories with ourselves&nbsp; when someone does or says something. They're not&nbsp;&nbsp; forced upon you by others. Others don't make you&nbsp; mad. You make yourself mad. And it's a bit of a&nbsp;&nbsp; mind twist, but oh my God, so true. So make sure&nbsp; that you're in charge of the story that is going&nbsp;&nbsp; on in your head. Is it the full story? Is it&nbsp; a true story? By learning to control emotions,&nbsp;&nbsp; you'll be better positioned to have a successful&nbsp; crucial conversation. Remember that emotions&nbsp;&nbsp; don't just happen, and you can either control&nbsp; your emotions or be controlled by them. &nbsp; Here's a neat little tactic to help you become&nbsp; the master of your emotions.

It is called&nbsp;&nbsp; retracing your path to action. It's essentially&nbsp; going back from how you acted. It goes like this.&nbsp;&nbsp; First, you start with the act. Examine your&nbsp; behavior. Ask yourself, how am I acting right&nbsp;&nbsp; now? Then you move on to the feeling. Identify the&nbsp; feeling. Ask yourself, what are the exact emotions&nbsp;&nbsp; that are driving the above behavior? Then you move&nbsp; on to the story. Ask yourself, what story that&nbsp;&nbsp; I'm telling myself is creating these emotions?&nbsp; And finally, examine the facts. Ask yourself,&nbsp;&nbsp; what is the evidence, things that you see or hear,&nbsp; that support the story?

By retracing your path,&nbsp;&nbsp; you can see exactly what is going on, hence&nbsp; gaining control over it in order to change your&nbsp;&nbsp; emotion, if needed. It is a phenomenal exercise.&nbsp; It's hard to do it at first, but the more you do&nbsp;&nbsp; it, the more you're going to discover how powerful&nbsp; it is in changing your own emotional state. &nbsp; Step number five is share your stories. Now that&nbsp; you're the ultimate master of your emotions,&nbsp;&nbsp; it is time to share your stories in a&nbsp; way that makes others receptive to them,&nbsp;&nbsp; in a way that encourages feedback.

Share your&nbsp; facts. Explain what conclusion you're drawing.&nbsp;&nbsp; Encourage the other person to do the&nbsp; same, share their story and their facts.&nbsp;&nbsp; And state your story as a story, not as a fact,&nbsp; and we've all been guilty of this. Your story&nbsp;&nbsp; is your story. It is not a fact of life. And&nbsp; encourage testing. Proactively seek other views&nbsp;&nbsp; that you can test your theory against. That was about your story. Next,&nbsp;&nbsp; you need to understand the other side. So&nbsp; step number six is explore the other's path.&nbsp;&nbsp; You need to carefully listen and try to understand&nbsp; the other person's viewpoint.

It is not easy,&nbsp;&nbsp; I know, but it's absolutely essential. Try&nbsp; to trace their path to action, same as you&nbsp;&nbsp; did earlier for yourself. Express an interest in&nbsp; their views, acknowledge their emotions, restate&nbsp;&nbsp; what you've heard and understood, and if the other&nbsp; person is holding back, use the priming technique.&nbsp;&nbsp; Offering a guess as to what they might be thinking&nbsp; is a way to get the discussion started. &nbsp; And now, for the final piece of the puzzle, step&nbsp; number seven, move the conversation to results.&nbsp;&nbsp; Once everybody contributes the information to a&nbsp; crucial conversation, the final step is action.&nbsp;&nbsp; All the conversation effort is dull, unless there&nbsp; is a plan of action and follow through to achieve&nbsp;&nbsp; results.

Make assignments, who will do what&nbsp; and when. Follow through. Agree on how and&nbsp;&nbsp; when you'll follow up on the agreed assignments.&nbsp; And finally, document. Language is our first tool, our first technology, the very thing that makes us human. And it’s a kind of power, a power that’s frequently misunderstood and poorly used. Most conversations involve little risk. We go about our days chatting, discussing, working, connecting, agreeing, and then every so often we encounter conflict. The boss shuts down your idea. Your direct report refuses. Your child disobeys. It’s in the face of disagreement where people struggle most to communicate effectively. And it’s in the face of disagreement where we have the greatest opportunity to influence the outcomes we care about.

You can strengthen relationships and get better results through communication. It largely depends on how well you handle Crucial Conversations.

What Makes Conversations Break Down? | Separate Facts Feelings and Identity
MindScience 360 · 7:34 · 15 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,520 words

A single remark in a meeting can transform a routine update into a tense exchange within seconds. Both people replay the moment, trying to prove what happened, and trust becomes harder to rebuild. These discussions often go off track because they blend facts, feelings, and identity questions without clearly naming the mix. One side argues details, while the other reacts to the meaning, respect, and what the moment implies about character. The result is distance, as each person defends their own story and stops taking in new information. Small misunderstandings can escalate into large conflicts when blame, hurt, and self-protection become the hidden goal.

A workable approach starts by treating the conversation as a learning task rather than a courtroom debate. That shift creates space for clearer listening, clearer speaking, and choices that improve the relationship afterward. In the next minutes, you will map three layers, replace blame with contribution, and express feelings without losing composure. This video is inspired by Difficult Conversations by Douglas Stone and Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen, and subscribe for calmer ways to handle conflict. Every difficult conversation contains three layers: the What Happened layer, the Feelings layer, and the Identity layer.

Each layer asks a different question, so missing one can distort the entire conversation. When only facts are debated, emotions remain unaddressed, and identity concerns linger in the background. This creates defensiveness, as each person feels unheard and focuses on winning rather than understanding. Two coworkers can describe the same project mistake, yet report different causes, motives, and responsibilities. Without recognizing these layers, responses often sound like denial, causing conflicts to escalate even when goals overlap. By seeing these three layers, it becomes easier to separate disagreements about events from disagreements about meaning.

This also keeps the conversation on track, making the real problem clearer and less personal. Try identifying which layer is active now and ask a question that fits that layer. Then, summarize what you heard in one sentence and check if you missed any feelings or identity concerns. The What Happened layer often begins with the assumption of truth, meaning each side believes their story is the full truth. Perception is the mechanism, as people select different facts and then add interpretations that feel obvious. When the focus shifts to proving who is right, curiosity fades and the conversation turns into a battle of messages.

Shifting to a learning stance means exploring how each story was built and what each person is trying to protect. Intentions create extra heat because they are invisible, so people often invent them from the impact. This invention hardens judgments, as a mistake is treated like a deliberate insult or a sign of disrespect. A third story viewpoint helps by describing the difference between stories without deciding who is right. From there, each person can share the impact, clarify purpose, and test assumptions with real questions. Ask what information the other person might be using that you do not see yet.

Also state what you are uncertain about, since uncertainty invites explanation instead of defense. Blame feels natural, but contribution is the more useful frame for changing what keeps repeating. The mechanism is interaction, because outcomes usually grow from both sides’ actions, reactions, and missed signals. Contribution is not a moral judgment; it is a map of how the pattern formed and where leverage exists. Starting from the third story means describing the gap and its effects, then exploring how each person contributed. A manager can push for faster output while giving unclear priorities, and an employee can stay silent and guess.

Both actions feed the same failure cycle, and focusing on one villain blocks practical improvement. Contribution lowers defensiveness, because accountability becomes specific behaviors rather than sweeping character verdicts. It also supports problem solving, because each person can choose one change within their control immediately. List your own contributions first, including what you did, what you avoided, and what you assumed without checking. If mapping contributions helps, subscribe to more wording that keeps accountability clear while protecting respect and trust. The Feelings layer is crucial because it shapes what people notice, remember, and defend during conflict.

The mechanism is that unspoken feelings do not vanish; they leak through tone, timing, and withdrawal. When feelings are dismissed, the conversation stays stuck on surface facts and never resolves the real hurt. Carefully naming feelings can reduce confusion, as it explains reactions without turning them into accusations. A coworker might say a decision was fine, but their voice carries disappointment, making the next collaboration strained. Another person might push harder on facts, which the first person hears as a lack of interest in their experience. Feelings are also clues, as they often point to values like respect, fairness, safety, or belonging.

Sharing these values helps the other person understand why the issue matters beyond the immediate event. Start by identifying what you feel and what you want the other person to understand about that feeling. Then invite their feelings too, as mutual acknowledgment makes later problem solving possible. The Identity layer explores how a situation defines who you are as a person. The mechanism involves all-or-nothing thinking, where a single mistake feels like proof of incompetence or unworthiness. When identity feels threatened, feedback sounds like an attack, and even neutral facts can sting sharply.

A more balanced identity includes strengths and weaknesses, so criticism becomes information rather than a verdict. Good listening supports this balance when you adopt curiosity and ask the other person to help you understand. Authentic listening means the stance matters, not just paraphrasing, because people can sense whether curiosity is real. One practical step is summarizing their story and feelings, then checking your summary until they feel heard. Once they feel heard, they become more able to hear your impact and your requests without interruption. Notice the commentator in your head and name it silently, so it stops pulling attention away from listening.

Then speak from your identity complexity, admitting what is true and what you still value about yourself. Hard conversations become manageable when treated as three layers rather than one argument. Stories, feelings, and identity pressures can be directly named, reducing confusion and making choices clearer. Adopting a learning stance replaces the need to win, opening space to understand how each story was built. Contribution replaces blame, allowing both parties to change the pattern without assigning permanent fault. Expressing feelings and values makes impact visible, so respect and repair become realistic goals.

Keeping identity balanced prevents collapse into shame, making accountability possible without panic. Start small by choosing one upcoming issue and writing the third story description in neutral language. Then plan one question to learn their story and one sentence to share your impact with a steady tone. When progress happens, it comes from repeated practice, not one perfect conversation. If these tools make hard talks manageable, subscribe for more guided practice prompts that build calm and clarity.

Shannon's Information Entropy (Physical Analogy)
Art of the Problem · 7:05 · 155,819 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~1,041 words

Imagine 2 machines. They both output messages from an alphabet of A, B, C, or D. Machine 1 generates each symbol randomly. They all occur 25% of the time. Machine 2 generates symbols according to the following probabilities. Now, which machine is producing more information? Claude Shannon cleverly rephrased the question. If you had to predict the next symbol from each machine, what is the minimum number of yes or no questions you would expect to ask? Let's look at Machine 1. The most efficient way is to pose a question which divides the possibilities in half. For example, our first question, we could ask if it is any 2 symbols-- such as, is it A or B?

Since there is a 50% chance of A or B and a 50% chance of C or D. After getting the answer, we can eliminate half of the possibilities. And we will be left with 2 symbols, both equally likely. So we simply pick one-- such as, is it A? And after this second question, we will have correctly identified the symbol. So we can say the uncertainty of Machine 1 is 2 questions per symbol. Now, what about Machine 2? As with Machine 1, we could ask two questions to determine the next symbol. However, this time the probability of each symbol is different. So we can ask our questions differently. Here A has a 50% chance of occurring, and all other letters add to 50%.

So we could start by asking-- Is it A? If it is A, we are done. Only one question in this case. Otherwise, we are left with 2 equal outcomes-- D or B and C. So we could ask-- is it D? If yes, we are done with 2 questions. Otherwise, we have to ask a third question to identify which of the last 2 symbols it is. On average, how many questions do you expect to ask to determine a symbol from Machine 2? And this can be explained nicely with an analogy. Let's assume instead we want to build Machine 1 and Machine 2. And we can generate symbols by bouncing a disk off a peg into 1 of 2 equally likely directions.

Based on which way it falls, we can generate a symbol. So with Machine 1, we need to add a second level or a second bounce so that we have 2 bounces, which lead to 4 equally likely outcomes. And based on where the disk lands, we output A, B, C, or D. Now, Machine 2. In this case, the first bounce leads to either an A-- which occurs 50% of the time-- or else we lead to a second bounce, which then can either output at D-- which occurs 25% of the time-- or else it leads to a third bounce, which then leads to either B or C-- 12.5% of the time. So now we just take a weighted average as follows-- the expected number of bounces is the probability of symbol A times 1 bounce plus the probability of B times 3 bounces plus the probability of C times 3 bounces plus the probability of D times 2 bounces.

And this works out to 1.75 bounces. Now, notice the connection between yes or no questions and fair bounces. The expected number of questions is equal to the expected number of bounces. So Machine 1 requires 2 bounces to generate a symbol while guessing an unknown symbol requires 2 questions. Machine 2 requires 1.75 bounces. We need to ask 1.75 questions on average. Meaning, if we need to guess 100 symbols from both machines, we can expect to ask 200 questions for Machine 1 and 175 questions for Machine 2. So this means that Machine 2 is producing less information because there is less uncertainty or surprise about its output.

And that's it. Claude Shannon calls this measure of average uncertainty "entropy," and he uses a letter H to represent it. And the unit of entropy Shannon chooses is based on the uncertainty of a fair coin flip, and he calls this "the bit," which is equivalent to a fair bounce. And we can arrive at the same result using our bounce analogy. Entropy, or H, is the summation for each symbol of the probability of that symbol times the number of bounces. Now, the difference is-- how do we express number of bounces in a more general way? And as we've seen, number of bounces depends how far down the tree we are.

And we can simplify this by saying that the number of bounces equals the logarithm base 2 of the number of outcomes at that level. And the number of outcomes at a level is also based on the probability, where the number of outcomes at a level equals 1 divided by the probability of that outcome. Number of bounces actually equals the logarithm base 2 of 1 over the probability of that symbol, which gives us our final equation. Entropy, or H, is the summation for each symbol of the probability of that symbol times the logarithm base 2 of 1 over the probability of that symbol. And Shannon writes this slightly different, which just inverts the expression inside the logarithm, which causes us to add a negative, though both formulas give the same results.

So let's summarize. Entropy is maximum when all outcomes are equally likely. Any time you move away from equally likely outcomes or introduce predictability, the entropy must go down. Now, the fundamental idea is that if the entropy of an information source drops, that means we can ask fewer questions to guess the outcome. And thanks to Shannon, the bit-- which is the unit of entropy-- is adopted as our quantitative measure of information or measure of surprise.
